articleInfo.subtitle: Carbon credits are the financial instrument behind the global effort to price emissions. Here is everything you need to understand them — from what a single credit actually represents to why India just launched its own trading scheme.

introduction.content:
Most people have heard of carbon credits. Far fewer can explain what one actually is.

That is a problem — because carbon credits are no longer a niche environmental instrument. They are becoming a legal compliance requirement for hundreds of Indian businesses, a line item in CFO budgets, and a traded financial asset on regulated exchanges.

This article explains what a carbon credit is, how one gets created, who buys them and why, and what India's new Carbon Credit Trading Scheme means for your organisation. No jargon. No fluff. Just what you need to know.

sections.heading: What Is a Carbon Credit?
sections.content:
A carbon credit is a certificate that represents the verified reduction or removal of one metric tonne of carbon dioxide — or its equivalent in other greenhouse gases — from the Earth's atmosphere.

Three words in that definition matter: verified, reduction, and equivalent.

Verified means an independent auditor has confirmed the reduction actually happened. It is not a promise or a plan. Someone checked the numbers.

Reduction means one of two things: either an emission that would have occurred was prevented — a coal plant that switched to solar — or carbon already in the atmosphere was removed, such as through a forest restoration project.

Equivalent is what extends carbon credits beyond CO₂ alone. Methane, nitrous oxide, and other greenhouse gases each trap different amounts of heat. Scientists express all of them in terms of their CO₂-equivalent warming effect. So one carbon credit always equals one tonne of CO₂e — one tonne of carbon dioxide, or the warming equivalent of one tonne of CO₂ in any other gas.

In practice, one carbon credit is abbreviated as 1 CC, 1 VCU in the voluntary market, or 1 CCC (Carbon Credit Certificate) under India's CCTS.

infoBox.title: 1 Carbon Credit = 1 tCO₂e
infoBox.content: One carbon credit represents the verified reduction or removal of one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent from the atmosphere. It is a standardised unit — the same way one kilogram is a standard unit of weight, one carbon credit is a standard unit of verified climate action.

sections.heading: Why Carbon Credits Exist
sections.content:
When a factory releases CO₂, that gas does not stay above the factory. It mixes into the global atmosphere, where it contributes to warming everywhere on Earth. The climate system does not care where emissions came from.

This creates a market problem: the factory has no private financial incentive to reduce its emissions. The costs of climate change — extreme weather, rising seas, damaged crops — are shared across billions of people over decades. But the cost of reducing emissions falls entirely on the one facility making the reduction.

Economists call this an externality. Carbon credits are the mechanism designed to correct it — by creating a price for emitting CO₂. When a price exists, facilities that can reduce emissions cheaply have a reason to do so. And facilities that find reduction expensive can pay for reductions elsewhere, achieving the same atmospheric outcome at lower total cost.

This is the economic logic behind every carbon market in the world — from the EU Emissions Trading System to India's newly launched CCTS.

sections.heading: The Life Cycle of a Carbon Credit
sections.content:
A carbon credit is not issued by a government. It originates from a real-world project and goes through a structured process before becoming a tradeable instrument.

Step 1 — Project Design. A developer identifies an activity that will reduce emissions — a wind farm replacing coal, a mangrove restoration, a landfill capturing methane. They write a Project Design Document describing exactly how reductions will be measured.

Step 2 — Validation. An accredited third-party auditor reviews the project design and confirms it is credible — that the baseline is realistic and the reduction would not have happened without the carbon credit incentive.

Step 3 — Monitoring and Verification. Once operational, the project tracks its actual emission reductions. Another round of independent verification confirms that the reported reductions occurred. This process — Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification, or MRV — is the backbone of carbon credit credibility.

Step 4 — Issuance. A registry issues credits to the developer's account. Each credit gets a unique serial number recording its project origin, vintage year, and the standard under which it was issued.

Step 5 — Trading. The developer sells credits — directly to buyers or on an exchange. Credits can transfer multiple times before reaching their final owner.

Step 6 — Retirement. When a buyer uses a credit to offset their emissions, they retire it — a permanent action in the registry's ledger. A retired credit cannot be sold, transferred, or used again. This is what prevents double-counting.

infoBox.title: Retirement Is Permanent and Public
infoBox.content: The moment a carbon credit is retired, it is permanently cancelled. Most registries maintain public retirement databases — anyone can search them to verify that a company's claimed offsets are real and have not been sold twice.

sections.heading: Who Creates Carbon Credits?
sections.content:
Carbon credits are created by project developers — organisations that design, fund, and operate emission reduction projects. The main project types are:

Renewable Energy — a solar or wind project replacing fossil fuel electricity generation earns credits for the emissions it displaces.

Forestry and Land Use (REDD+) — projects that preserve forests from deforestation, or actively restore degraded land, earn credits as trees absorb CO₂.

Methane Capture — landfills, agricultural operations, and natural gas facilities that capture methane before it escapes into the atmosphere. Because methane is roughly 28 times more potent than CO₂, even modest methane capture generates substantial credits.

Industrial Efficiency — energy efficiency improvements in manufacturing facilities. Under India's CCTS, this is the primary pathway through which Indian industrial companies generate Carbon Credit Certificates.

Carbon Removal — newer technologies like biochar and direct air capture that physically extract CO₂ from the atmosphere. The most permanent form of credit, and currently the most expensive.

sections.heading: Who Buys Carbon Credits — and Why?
sections.content:
Carbon credit buyers fall into two distinct groups.

Compliance buyers are companies legally required to hold credits. If a government caps the emissions a facility can produce and that facility exceeds its cap, it must acquire credits to make up the shortfall — or pay a penalty. For compliance buyers, credits are not optional. They are a regulatory requirement, like a tax.

Voluntary buyers choose to purchase credits without a legal obligation. Their motivations include public net-zero commitments, supply chain decarbonisation requirements from larger customers, and ESG reporting pressures from investors. Airlines, technology companies, and consumer brands are among the largest voluntary buyers globally.

The distinction matters because it determines price sensitivity and urgency. A compliance buyer facing a regulatory deadline will pay what it takes. A voluntary buyer has more flexibility — but also more selectivity about the quality and story behind the credits they purchase.

infoBox.title: Carbon Credits Are Not a Licence to Keep Polluting
infoBox.content: A common misconception is that buying credits permits continued emissions. It does not. Credits are intended for emissions a company cannot yet eliminate — after genuine reduction efforts. Using credits to avoid emission reductions entirely is what greenwashing means, and it is increasingly scrutinised by regulators and investors.

sections.heading: India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme
sections.content:
In June 2023, India's Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) notified the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) under the Energy Conservation Act — creating India's first mandatory domestic carbon market.

Unlike the EU's hard cap system, India's CCTS uses Greenhouse Gas Emission Intensity (GEI) targets — measuring emissions per unit of output rather than total emissions. A steel plant, for example, might have a target of emitting no more than X tonnes of CO₂ per tonne of crude steel. Outperform the target, earn Carbon Credit Certificates (CCCs) to sell. Miss the target, buy CCCs or pay a penalty.

Nine industrial sectors are currently covered: Iron & Steel, Cement, Aluminium, Fertilisers, Petroleum Refineries, Petrochemicals, Paper & Pulp, Chlor-Alkali, and Textiles. CCCs trade on IEX and PXIL within a regulated price band of ₹600 to ₹1,200 per certificate, under oversight from CERC. GRID-India maintains the official registry.

For facilities in these nine sectors, this is not a future obligation. The baseline period is underway. If your company has not yet begun tracking emission intensity by facility, you are already behind.

infoBox.title: Is Your Company a BEE Designated Consumer?
infoBox.content: If your facility operates in any of the nine CCTS sectors and meets the energy consumption threshold, you have pending GEI compliance obligations. The baseline period is active now. A dedicated guide to the CCTS — covering sector-specific targets, registry mechanics, and exchange trading — is coming in the next article.

sections.heading: How EtherTrack Fits In
sections.content:
EtherTrack is building the digital infrastructure that India's carbon market currently lacks.

Right now, most Indian businesses track emissions in spreadsheets, navigate credit purchases through brokers, assemble regulatory reports manually at significant cost, and receive retirement certificates as PDFs with no independent verification pathway.

EtherTrack connects all of this in one platform. Emission data entered once — via manual entry, CSV, ERP sync, or AI parser — automatically feeds your GHG inventory, your carbon credit gap calculation, and your regulatory reports (BRSR Core, CDP, TCFD, and GHG Protocol) simultaneously. No reconciliation. No consultant.

On the trading side, the platform offers a live order book and hybrid AMM liquidity pool for buying and selling carbon credits, with payment in Indian Rupees via UPI, card, or bank transfer. Every retirement generates an ISO 14064-3 certificate with a QR code that resolves to a permanent on-chain record — verifiable by any auditor, independently, without contacting us.

For CCTS-covered facilities, a dedicated compliance module tracks GEI positions plant by plant, runs intra-group netting calculations, and routes orders to IEX or PXIL.

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: A carbon credit represents the verified reduction or removal of exactly one metric tonne of CO₂ equivalent. It is not a promise — an independent auditor has confirmed it happened.
Carbon credits exist to create a financial price for emissions, aligning private incentives with the public interest in emission reduction.
Every credit goes through a structured life cycle: project design → validation → monitoring and verification (MRV) → issuance → trading → permanent retirement.
Compliance buyers are legally required to hold credits. Voluntary buyers choose to purchase them for net-zero commitments, ESG reporting, or supply chain requirements.

India's CCTS — notified in 2023 — is a mandatory compliance market covering nine industrial sectors. GEI targets are already active. Facilities that outperform earn sellable CCCs; those that miss must buy or pay penalties.
Carbon credits are not a licence to keep polluting. They are intended for emissions a business cannot yet eliminate — after genuine reduction efforts.

faqs.question: What is a carbon credit in simple terms?
faqs.answer: A carbon credit is a certificate proving that one tonne of greenhouse gas has been prevented from entering — or removed from — the atmosphere. It has been independently measured, verified, and registered. Companies buy and retire credits to compensate for their own emissions they cannot yet eliminate.

faqs.question: What is 1 carbon credit worth in India?
faqs.answer: Under India's CCTS, Carbon Credit Certificates trade within a regulated band of ₹600 to ₹1,200 per credit. In the voluntary market, prices vary by project quality — from roughly ₹400 for older renewable energy credits to ₹2,500 or more for high-quality nature-based or Article 6-authorised credits.

faqs.question: Who regulates carbon credits in India?
faqs.answer: The CCTS is administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) under the Ministry of Power, with trading oversight from CERC. GRID-India maintains the Carbon Credit Certificate registry. Voluntary credits in India are regulated by international standards bodies — primarily Verra and Gold Standard.

faqs.question: What does retirement mean for a carbon credit?
faqs.answer: Retirement is the permanent cancellation of a credit in the registry's ledger. Once retired, a credit cannot be sold, transferred, or used again by anyone. This is what prevents double-counting. Most registries maintain public retirement databases that anyone can search to verify a retirement claim.

faqs.question: What are the nine sectors covered under India's CCTS?
faqs.answer: Iron & Steel, Cement, Aluminium, Fertilisers, Petroleum Refineries, Petrochemicals, Paper & Pulp, Chlor-Alkali, and Textiles. Facilities in these sectors that meet the energy consumption threshold will have mandatory GEI targets assigned.

faqs.question: What is MRV and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: MRV stands for Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification — the quality control process that confirms a carbon credit represents a real emission reduction. Without MRV, there is no way to know whether a reported reduction actually happened. Every credible carbon credit programme requires it before credits are issued.
